# Introduction

How do various countries vote in the United Nations General Assembly, how have their voting patterns evolved throughout time, and how similarly or differently do they view certain issues? Answering these questions (at a high level) is the focus of this analysis.

## Packages

We will use the **tidyverse**, **lubridate**, and **scales** packages for data wrangling and visualization, and the **DT** package for interactive display of tabular output, and the **unvotes** package for the data.

```{r}
#| label: load-packages
#| message: false
#| warning: false 

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(scales)
library(DT)
library(unvotes)
```



## Data

The data we're using originally come from the **unvotes** package. In the chunk below we modify the data by joining the various data frames provided in the package to help you get started with the analysis.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false 
unv <- unvotes::un_votes %>%
  inner_join(un_roll_calls, by = "rcid") %>%
  inner_join(un_roll_call_issues, by = "rcid")
```

# UN voting patterns

Let's create a data visualisation that displays how the voting record of the UK & NI changed over time on a variety of issues, and compares it to two other countries: US and Turkey.

```{r}
#| label: plot-yearly-yes-issue
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

unv %>%
  filter(country %in% c("United Kingdom", "United States", "Turkey")) %>%
  mutate(year = year(date)) %>%
  group_by(country, year, issue) %>%
  summarize(percent_yes = mean(vote == "yes")) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = year, y = percent_yes, color = country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~issue) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Percentage of 'Yes' votes in the UN General Assembly",
    subtitle = "1946 to 2019",
    y = "% Yes",
    x = "Year",
    color = "Country"
  )
```

**1. Compared to the United States and to the United kingdom, Turkey reports "yes" more often. Historically the United States has had the lowest percentage of "yes" votes, with the most deviation from the other two countries being in the year 2019. 


We can easily change which countries are being plotted by changing which countries the code above `filter`s for. Note that the country name should be spelled and capitalized exactly the same way as it appears in the data. See the [Appendix](#appendix) for a list of the countries in the data.


```{r}
#| label: plot-yearly-yes-issue2
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

unv %>%
  filter(country %in% c("Mexico", "Guatemala", "Japan")) %>%
  mutate(year = year(date)) %>%
  group_by(country, year, issue) %>%
  summarize(percent_yes = mean(vote == "yes")) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = year, y = percent_yes, color = country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~issue) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Percentage of 'Yes' votes in the UN General Assembly",
    subtitle = "1946 to 2019",
    y = "% Yes",
    x = "Year",
    color = "Country"
  )
```


When compared to Japan, Guatemala and Mexico have had a higher percentage of "yes" votes. Overtime Guatemala and Mexico have had similar "yes" percentages. Over the years, the "yes" percentage in Japan has not been as constant as Guatemala and Mexico have been. The most similarity in "yes" percentage from all three countries is seen in colonialism.
